_meta.source: World Bank Commodity Markets Outlook (Oct 2015 special feature 'Understanding El Niño'), FAO Food Price Index, and the peer-reviewed ENSO-economics literature. Every row carries its citation.
_meta.method: NOTHING HERE IS FITTED BY THIS PROJECT. These are figures published elsewhere, transcribed with their source and sorted into four tiers that are never blended: (1) what the historical record shows, (2) what published models estimate, (3) what is genuinely contested, (4) where the damage actually lands.
_meta.why_this_file_exists: The El Niño panel has always refused to model a world price, for good reasons stated in data/enso_exposure.json's _meta.why_no_price. That refusal is correct and is kept. But refusing to MODEL a price is not the same as refusing to REPORT what the record and the literature say, and a reader asking 'what does this do to prices' deserves the evidence rather than silence. This file supplies the evidence; the page presents it as evidence, not as a forecast.
_meta.headline: A strong El Niño has historically meant a severe regional food-security emergency and has NOT historically meant a rise in world cereal prices. In the three strongest events on record, world wheat and maize prices fell. Whether a regional shock becomes a global price shock has depended on stocks, export policy and energy prices -- not on the strength of the El Niño.
_meta.sample_size_caveat: Six El Niño events and one multi-year La Niña. Two (2018-19, 2009-10) were too weak for a global signal to be expected; one (2015-16) is extraordinary; one (1982-83) predates the FAO Food Price Index entirely. Any claim of the form 'an El Niño of ONI +X historically produces Y' rests on three to five observations and must be given as a range with the events named, never as a fitted number. ONI itself is revisable -- 2018-19 is weak on ERSSTv5 and moderate on v6.

record.title: What the record shows
record.claim: Of six completed El Niño episodes between 1980 and 2014, the six-month average agricultural price index rose in only one — 2002-03.
record.source: World Bank, Commodity Markets Outlook, October 2015, special feature 'Understanding El Niño' (Baffes et al., Prospects Group).
record.quote: [There have been] six such episodes since 1980 (excluding the ongoing one) ... in only one case (2002-03) the six-month average agricultural price index leading to the episode increased modestly... In all other cases, prices either declined (1982-83) or changed very little.
record.figure: Figure F.8, Commodity Markets Outlook, October 2015
record.figure_note: Verbatim from the figure: “The numbers denote percent changes of the six-month average price index leading to the episode compared to the previous six-month period (bold) and the corresponding six-month period of the previous year (italic). The last observation for both agricultural price index and El Niño is September 2015.”
record.peaks_note: Seven ENSO peaks are annotated on the figure: the six completed episodes since 1980 plus the event that was still ongoing when the report went to press in October 2015. The figure plots its labels against a time axis rather than naming each episode, so only the three the text names — 1982-83, 1997-98 and 2002-03 — can be attached to a peak with confidence. This panel therefore shows the distribution and names only those three. An earlier cut of this file invented year labels for all seven and mis-assigned the −14.8 reading to 1997-98 when it belongs to the then-ongoing 2015 event; that was a transcription error, corrected here against the source PDF.

named.1982-83: One of the two deepest declines on the figure.
named.1997-98: The strongest event in the instrumental record at the time. Prices did not rise.
named.2002-03: The single episode the text identifies as a rise: +10.4% against the previous six months, +9.8% year-on-year.

ffpi.title: The FAO Food Price Index at El Niño peak years
ffpi.source: FAO Food Price Index, annual averages, base 2014-2016 = 100.
ffpi.note: The 2015-16 event was the strongest in the instrumental record. In January 2016 the FAO index fell to a near seven-year low, down 16% year on year -- FAO's own headline was 'FAO Food Price Index starts 2016 dropping to nearly 7-year low'. The World Bank had predicted exactly this in November 2015, before the peak.
ffpi.gap: Exact 1980s FFPI point values for the 1982-83 and 1986-87 episodes could not be independently verified; those two episodes are represented only by the World Bank's percentage changes above.

models.title: What published models estimate
models.preamble: These are conditional estimates from published models. They do not contradict the record above -- a model can correctly estimate an average conditional effect that is then swamped in most individual years by ordinary supply variation. Both facts are true and the page shows both.

rows.finding: A 1-sd ENSO surprise raises real non-oil commodity price inflation by 3.5-4 pp for 6-12 months; ENSO accounts for about 20% of commodity price inflation variance and 10-20% of world CPI inflation movements.
rows.source: Brunner 2002, Review of Economics and Statistics 84(1):176-183
rows.caveat: The most-cited number here and the most over-extended. It is a BROAD NON-OIL COMMODITY index, not a food index, and it is an unexpected-shock elasticity, not an event average.

rows.finding: A typical El Niño raises real non-fuel commodity prices 5.31% cumulated over four quarters; oil +13.87%.
rows.source: Cashin, Mohaddes & Raissi 2017, Journal of International Economics 106:37-54 (IMF WP/15/89)
rows.caveat: A broad basket, not cereals. The same paper finds El Niño is growth-ENHANCING for the US, Europe and China.

rows.finding: A strong El Niño raises global food commodity prices by up to 9%, peaking about 16 months after onset. Soybeans, maize and rice show pronounced upside; wheat is positive but statistically insignificant; coffee and cocoa near zero.
rows.source: World Bank Commodity Markets Outlook Oct 2023, via ECB Economic Bulletin box, June 2023
rows.caveat: The World Bank Oct 2023 primary text was not independently verified in this compilation; the ECB box is the traced source.

rows.finding: ENSO shocks move prices 1-5% and explain 15-30% of price variation at 1-2 year horizons -- but ONLY for vegetable oils and protein meals, wheat, soybeans, beef, salmon and Arabica coffee. Barley, maize and sorghum show NO causal linkage. The effect has been mitigated over time.
rows.source: Ubilava 2018, American Journal of Agricultural Economics 100(1):239-263
rows.caveat: Palm and vegetable oils are the strongest and most consistent channel of any commodity.

rows.finding: Wheat prices tend to RISE after La Niña and FALL after El Niño, with amplified and more persistent responses in the La Niña regime -- consistent with low-inventory storage economics.
rows.caveat: This is the opposite sign to the popular story, and it is the finding most often left out of El Niño coverage.

contested.title: Where the literature genuinely disagrees
contested.preamble: Two peer-reviewed literatures estimate the macroeconomic cost of El Niño and reach conclusions that differ by an order of magnitude AND, for the United States, in sign. The page shows both. It does not average them and does not pick a winner.

positions.method: Panel/local-projection regression on 1960-2019 country GDP, modelling El Niño as producing persistent, compounding GROWTH-rate effects lasting 5+ years.

figures.v: $4.1 trillion cumulative global income loss over the following 5 years
$84 trillion cumulative, even under current emissions pledges
GDP about 3% LOWER five years after the event

positions.side: Small, transient, and positive for rich importers
positions.source: Cashin, Mohaddes & Raissi 2017, J. Int. Econ. 106:37-54 (IMF WP/15/89)
positions.method: Global VAR across 21 country/region models, 1979Q2-2013Q1; shock is a 1-sd fall in the Southern Oscillation Index.

figures.v: GDP growth +0.55% cumulated at 4 quarters — a GAIN

positions.mechanism: Effect size tracks each country's primary-sector share of GDP — Indonesia 25%, Peru 20%, India 21%, against the US at 3% and Japan at 1%.

critiques.what: "We are skeptical of these results." The implied cumulative global GDP scarring from each event exceeds Oxford Economics' own estimate of COVID-19 scarring. Global natural-disaster damage to property, crops and livestock ran at only 0.2% of global GDP a year in the three years to 2021, with no clear uptick during past intense El Niño phases.
Challenges the aggregate framing directly — not all countries suffer, and his own work finds El Niño growth-enhancing for the US and Europe.

Methodological: 'growth effects' specifications of the kind used here produce wildly divergent long-run projections against 'level effects' specifications — a 95% interval spanning 84% GDP losses to 359% gains by 2100 — because of a stock-flow mismatch that can mechanically manufacture permanent effects from transient shocks.

contested.corroboration: For the United States specifically, Changnon (1999) costed the 1997-98 event directly and found a NET BENEFIT of $15 bn — $4 bn of costs against $19 bn of benefits, about 0.2% of US GDP. That is independent support for the IMF side of this disagreement.

local.title: Where the damage actually lands
local.preamble: The transmission that matters for food security is local, not global. Weather shocks have robust short-run effects on domestic staple prices in developing countries, while only a small share of those markets track world prices in the short run. This is why world indices can fall while a household's maize price doubles.
local.source: World Bank Commodity Markets Outlook 2015, citing Brown & Kshirsagar 2015.

cases.note: While world grain prices were soft.
Against a backdrop of falling world cereal prices.
Driven by India's July 2023 non-basmati export ban, not by the harvest itself. The FAO cereal index FELL in the same period; rice was the one grain that rose, and it rose on POLICY.

policy_amplifier.claim: Trade policy is a bigger price amplifier than the weather.
policy_amplifier.evidence: Insulating policies during 2010-11 accounted for about 40% of the world wheat price rise and about 25% of maize. El Niño years reliably trigger export restrictions — Zambia 2016 and 2024, Tanzania 2023, India non-basmati rice 2023.
policy_amplifier.source: World Bank Commodity Markets Outlook, April 2019, special focus

local.conditioning: 2015-16 is the proof: the strongest El Niño in the instrumental record, a 40-million-person regional emergency, and a seven-year low in the FAO Food Price Index in the same month -- because stocks were ample, oil was cheap and no major exporter restricted trade. 2007-08 is the inverse: barely any weather, and the largest price spike on record, because stocks were thin and seven governments restricted trade at once.

do_not_publish.title: Claims in circulation that this page will not make
do_not_publish.preamble: Each of these is widely repeated and each failed verification. They are listed so a reader can check this dashboard against the coverage they have already seen.

rows.claim: "El Niño causes global food price spikes."
rows.verdict: The sign is often backwards. Ubilava 2017 finds wheat prices rise after La Niña and fall after El Niño. Both modern price spikes (2007-08, 2010-11) peaked during La Niña.

rows.claim: "The 2007-08 and 2010-11 food crises were El Niño events."
rows.verdict: 2007-08 peaked at ONI −1.76, a strong La Niña. It is assigned to biofuel demand, oil, the dollar, low stocks-to-use and export bans. 2010-11 traces to Russia's heatwave and its 5 August 2010 export ban.

rows.claim: "The 1982-83 El Niño cost over US$8 billion and ~2,000 lives."
rows.verdict: UNTRACED. The figure traces to a UCAR/NOAA popular booklet with no method or citation; the '$8.7 bn / 1,100 lives' pairing traces to National Geographic (1984). Not published here.

rows.claim: "The 1997-98 El Niño caused ~$33-36 bn and 21,000-23,000 deaths."
rows.verdict: UNTRACED. Traces to a Science news item (Kerr 1999) and an unpublished NOAA draft (Sponberg 1999) whose own citing paper warns the estimates 'should not be taken as absolute measures of loss.'

rows.claim: "1982-83 was the strongest El Niño on record."
rows.verdict: True when written, false today. On the current ONI it ranks third, behind 2015-16 and 1997-98.

rows.claim: "Indonesian rice production fell 18% in 2023-24 due to El Niño."
rows.verdict: Traced only to trade press. No BPS or FAO confirmation. IFPRI's assessment was 'less than feared.'

rows.claim: "The 2023 Amazon drought was the El Niño drought."
rows.verdict: World Weather Attribution splits the rainfall deficit roughly evenly between El Niño and climate change, and finds the record severity almost entirely driven by warming, not by the Pacific.

rows.claim: "The 2023 Mississippi low-water crisis was caused by El Niño."
rows.verdict: It coincided with a strong El Niño but is not attributed to it. The textbook teleconnection would have made the lower basin wetter. Attributed instead to a summer heat dome.

rows.claim: "The 2023-24 cocoa price spike was an El Niño story."
rows.verdict: ICCO's own materials co-attribute the shock to black-pod disease and aging trees. December 2023 EXCESS rainfall caused the rot; dry Harmattan heat followed. Not a clean single-cause event.

Often the reverse. El Niño brings warmer Brazilian winters, which REDUCES frost risk — and frost is the classic arabica shock. Robusta in Vietnam is the strong, direct link; do not lump the two together.

rows.claim: "86 million sheep and 14 million cattle died in the 1982-83 Australian drought."
rows.verdict: Arithmetically impossible — it exceeds Australia's entire national flock. Almost certainly 'were in drought-declared areas.'
